analysis.one_liner: Moves Medicare's drug price negotiations and $2,000 out-of-pocket drug cap forward two years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in any House committee before Congress ended, and it drew no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the dates on two Medicare drug-cost provisions already enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act. It would have let Medicare start negotiating prices for selected high-cost drugs in 2024 instead of 2026, with each later round of negotiations also starting two years sooner. It would also have applied the $2,000 annual cap on what Medicare patients pay out of pocket for prescription drugs starting the next year, rather than in 2025. It was referred to two committees, then to a health subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use expensive prescription drugs. They would have hit the $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap a year sooner, and negotiated prices on selected drugs would have arrived two years earlier, lowering the list prices Medicare pays and, over time, what patients are charged.

how_it_helps.text: The bill moves the Medicare Part D annual out-of-pocket threshold forward so the redesigned benefit — including the $2,000 annual cap on drug costs — applies in 2024 rather than 2025.

It moves the Medicare drug price negotiation program forward two years: the first round of negotiation would begin in 2024 instead of 2026, with each later round (through 2027-2028) also starting two years sooner.
It makes conforming date changes throughout the Part D statute so the earlier negotiation schedule and the earlier out-of-pocket cap line up with existing plan-year rules.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would have lost two years of selling selected top-selling drugs at un-negotiated prices before Medicare negotiation kicked in. Medicare Part D plan sponsors would also have had to implement the redesigned benefit, with its $2,000 cap and elimination of the coverage-gap phase, a year earlier than planned.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D plans

drawbacks.text: Compressing the timeline creates real implementation risk. Medicare drug plans set their annual bids and build their pharmacy networks and cost-sharing rules many months before the plan year starts, so moving the $2,000 cap up a year would have forced mid-stream changes to plans that were already designed and priced under the old schedule.

The bill changes dates but does nothing else: it adds no new enforcement tools or additional protections, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that speed alone strains the negotiation program, which requires the government to select drugs, gather data, and negotiate within a fixed calendar that was already considered aggressive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare patients with high drug costs, the benefit is concrete and near-term: a $2,000 cap a year sooner and negotiated prices arriving two years earlier. The costs fall almost entirely on brand-name drug manufacturers in the form of two fewer years of full monopoly pricing on selected drugs, plus some administrative strain on Medicare plans from the compressed timeline. On balance the bill would have shifted money from drug companies to patients using policy tools that were already law; its main weakness is that it was written only as a set of date changes, leaving the operational squeeze unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever held a hearing or markup or sent it to the floor before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Seth Magaziner introduced the bill in the House on October 11, 2023, as a one-sponsor bill with no cosponsors.
On October 25, 2023, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee.
It was then referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on November 3, 2023, and again on December 17, 2024, and never advanced past that point.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House, and no Senate action of any kind is recorded; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: under the existing schedule they keep two more years of un-negotiated prices on selected drugs before Medicare negotiation begins, and Medicare patients wait longer for the $2,000 out-of-pocket cap. The committee leaders who left the bill without action also avoided the rework that an accelerated timeline would have required of Medicare plans.

for.name: Rep. Seth Magaziner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to accelerate Medicare's drug price negotiation timeline and the $2,000 out-of-pocket cap.

against.name: Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 25, 2023 and sent it to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat through the end of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received a referral on October 25, 2023 over Medicare financing provisions and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority party of the 118th House
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists; the sponsor was a Democrat and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: Medicare negotiation arriving in 2024 instead of 2026 would cut two years off the window in which companies can charge un-negotiated prices on selected top-selling drugs, and the earlier $2,000 cap would reduce what beneficiaries pay in the interim. The industry's interest in keeping the original, later schedule runs directly against patients' interest in lower prices sooner.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plan sponsors would have had to rebuild their 2024 benefit designs a year early around the $2,000 cap and the elimination of the coverage-gap phase, raising administrative and bid-pricing risk. Because these intermediaries sit between Medicare's payments and patients' drug costs, an earlier arrival of the cap mostly narrows their room to absorb or pass through drug prices.
